## Preface {.unnumbered}

Yale's [Public Health Data Science and Data Equity (DSDE)](https://ysph.yale.edu/research/research-centers-and-initiatives/public-health-data-science-and-data-equity/) team hosts workshops, tutorials, and information sessions known as Coffee, Cookies, and Coding $\left(C^3\right)$ Workshops. These sessions are designed to help Public Health and Biostatistics masters-level students at Yale effectively leverage computational tools and analytical methods in their educational and professional endeavors. While primarily intended for the Yale community, all are welcome and encouraged to attend and benefit from our offerings.

You can find out more about past and upcoming work on our [website](https://ysph.yale.edu/public-health-research-and-practice/research-centers-and-initiatives/public-health-data-science-and-data-equity/events/). Additional tutorials will soon be available on our YouTube channel. If you are affiliated with Yale, you can set up an office hour appointment with one of our data scientists on our [Bookings Page](https://outlook.office365.com/book/DataScienceDataEquityOfficeHours@yale.edu/?ismsaljsauthenabled=true).

Each module adapted for asynchronous learning is presented as its own chapter. To help build your technical vocabulary, key terms and code commands/functions are highlighted throughout. They will appear as either 
<span class="text-term" 
  data-hover-text="Hovering gives the definition!">
  new terms</span> 
and
<span class="code-term" 
  data-hover-text="Hovering gives the definition!">
  new code commands/functions</span>, and hovering over them will display their definitions. Terms are consistently highlighted each time they appear in the chapter, and each page concludes with a glossary of all terms used on that page.

### Live Workshop Content

```{=html}
<details class="session-details">
  <summary>
    <div class="summary-content">
      <h2>Choosing Good Subsamples for Measuring New Variables</h2>
      <span class="arrow">&gt;</span>
    </div>
  </summary>
  
  <p><strong>Date Held:</strong>  Monday, February 3<sup>rd</sup>, 2025</p>
  
  <p>Find the session materials and other related content on the <a href="https://github.com/ysph-dsde/Thomas-Lumley-Workshops/">GitHub</a> page.</p>
  
  <div class="instructors">
    <h3>Instructor:</h3>
    <ul>
      <li><a href="https://profiles.auckland.ac.nz/t-lumley">Professor Thomas Lumley</a>, Chair in Biostatistics Statistics at the University of Auckland</li>
    </ul>
  </div>

  <div class="learning-goals">
    <h3>Learning Goals:</h3>
    <p>
      Researchers often want to add more measurements to an existing database. These might be new assays on stored specimens, or coding of free-text responses, or validation of EHR data against clinical notes. It is expensive to measure the new variables on everyone, so subsampling is attractive. It is possible to do much better than simple random sampling when measuring additional data: any information you already have can be used to identify the most informative records to measure. It's also possible to recover a lot of information from the records that are not chosen in the subsample. Software already exists in R to support most analyses you would want to do of the subsampled data.
    </p>
  </div>
</details>
```

```{=html}
<details class="session-details">
  <summary>
    <div class="summary-content">
      <h2>Analyzing Larger Data in R</h2>
      <span class="arrow">&gt;</span>
    </div>
  </summary>
  
  <p><strong>Date Held:</strong>  Tuesday, February 4<sup>th</sup>, 2025</p>
  
  <p>Find the session materials and other related content on the <a href="https://github.com/ysph-dsde/Thomas-Lumley-Workshops/">GitHub</a> page.</p>
  
  <div class="instructors">
    <h3>Instructor:</h3>
    <ul>
      <li><a href="https://profiles.auckland.ac.nz/t-lumley">Professor Thomas Lumley</a>, Chair in Biostatistics Statistics at the University of Auckland</li>
    </ul>
  </div>

  <div class="learning-goals">
    <h3>Learning Goals:</h3>
    <p>
      Even with growing computer power, researchers sometimes want to work with datasets that are much bigger than computer memory. The interfaces to allow selection, summarization, and aggregation of very large datasets from R are increasingly transparent and easy to set up. I will demonstrate simple analysis of large datasets in R. I will also show how some more complicated analyses can be partitioned between R and a database to exploit the advantages of both systems. I will primarily use duckdb, but I will refer to other large-data interfaces.
    </p>
  </div>
</details>
```
